content: An aortic aneurysm is a serious condition characterized by a balloon-like bulge in the aorta, the largest artery in the body that carries blood from the heart to the rest of the body. This condition can lead to life-threatening complications if not addressed. When an aortic aneurysm occurs, it can either dissect or rupture. A dissection happens when the force of blood flow causes the layers of the artery wall to split, allowing blood to leak between them. A rupture, on the other hand, occurs when the aneurysm bursts entirely, leading to internal bleeding. Both dissections and ruptures are the primary causes of death associated with aortic aneurysms. Aortic aneurysms are classified into two main types based on their location: 1. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm: This type occurs in the chest. It affects men and women equally and becomes more common with age. The primary causes include high blood pressure, sudden trauma, or inherited connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Symptoms may include sharp, sudden chest or upper back pain, shortness of breath, and difficulty breathing or swallowing. 2. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm: This type occurs below the chest and is more common than thoracic aortic aneurysms. It is more frequently seen in men, individuals aged 65 and older, and White populations compared to Black populations. The most common cause is atherosclerosis (hardening of the arteries), though infections or injuries can also lead to this condition. Abdominal aortic aneurysms often do not present symptoms, but when they do, they may include throbbing or deep pain in the back or side, as well as pain in the buttocks, groin, or legs. Aneurysms can also develop in other parts of the body. For example, a ruptured aneurysm in the brain can result in a stroke. Peripheral aneurysms, which occur in arteries outside the aorta (such as in the neck, groin, or behind the knees), are less likely to rupture or dissect but can lead to blood clots that may block blood flow. Several risk factors increase the likelihood of developing an aortic aneurysm. Smoking is the most significant behavioral risk factor. Other contributing factors include high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and atherosclerosis. Additionally, inherited connective tissue disorders like Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, as well as a family history of aortic aneurysms, can elevate the risk. Treatment for aortic aneurysms typically involves either medication or surgery. Medications are used to lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of aneurysm progression. Surgery may be necessary to repair or replace the affected portion of the aorta, depending on the size and severity of the aneurysm.
